archival_memory.research_experience: I've been involved in undergraduate research since the end of my sophomore year. It's been an eye-opening experience that has given me a glimpse into how knowledge is created in the tech world.
archival_memory.research_leap: I was initially hesitant to pursue research, but it turned out to be a great decision.
archival_memory.lab_description: The lab I'm in is an interdisciplinary space where computer scientists partner with scientists from various backgrounds, such as astronomy, environmental science, and neuroscience. We work with massive datasets, often tens of terabytes in size. My main task is to create front-end prototypes that present slices of data in dynamic, interactive dashboards. This involves using advanced JavaScript frameworks, D3.js for custom visualizations, and specialized libraries for volumetric rendering if we're dealing with 3D data.
archival_memory.first_project: The first research project I really got into was visualizing oceanic temperature changes over time for a climate study group. They had daily temperature readings from buoys across the Pacific, scattered across different servers. Our job was to aggregate and present the data in a coherent way to show patterns over months or years. I dove in headfirst, writing scripts to clean and unify the data, building a pipeline for near real-time updates, and designing interfaces that allowed researchers to zoom into specific regions or timeframes. Eventually, I co-authored my first paper on this system. It was surreal to see my name in an official publication, and it's one of my proudest moments in college.
archival_memory.current_research: My current research has pivoted to immersive analytics platforms, exploring how VR or AR technologies can enhance scientists' intuitive understanding of complex data. It's a leap from coding websites, as it involves experimenting with VR headsets, integrating with engines like Unity or Unreal, and efficiently streaming data into a 3D environment. It's cutting-edge, and it's exciting to forge my own path in this uncharted territory.
archival_memory.research_life: Research life is not just about coding away in a quiet corner. It's a lot of reading, especially when trying to solve a specific problem like rendering volumetric data in VR. I need to comb through conference proceedings and workshops to see if someone has already attempted something similar. It can be overwhelming, but over time, you learn to skim effectively by looking at the abstract, introduction, and conclusion to determine relevance. Occasionally, when I find something interesting, I share it with the lab and we discuss how we can incorporate that technique into our workflow.
archival_memory.interactions_with_grad_students: I interact with a lot of graduate students in the lab, both master's and PhD students. It can be intimidating at first because they're so deeply immersed in their niche fields, but it's also inspiring. One PhD student is developing a machine learning algorithm for on-the-fly compression of large datasets and integrating it with our VR platform. The idea is to only load a compressed representation of the data in VR until you zoom in. It's wild, but it's super practical for real-time performance. Working alongside him allows me to see how advanced theoretical concepts are applied in real-world scenarios. Some of our best brainstorming sessions happen spontaneously, like in the lab break room over coffee, where we hash out how we can offload processing to the GPU.
archival_memory.poster_presentations: I've had the opportunity to present at a few poster presentations at smaller symposiums around campus. It was a great experience, as it forced me to distill complex research into easy-to-understand visuals and talking points. Initially, I was nervous, but it turned out to be a friendly dialogue. People were genuinely interested in what I was doing. I even met a few folks from local startups who shared interesting perspectives on how VR for data visualization could benefit commercial industries like marketing analytics or architecture. It opened my eyes to how research can transition from academia to real-world applications.
archival_memory.publications: I've been fortunate enough to be a co-author on two workshop papers and I'm currently working on a larger conference submission to the IEEE Visualization Conference(IEEE VIS). We're conducting a user study comparing traditional 2D dashboards with an interactive VR environment. Our hypothesis is that VR immersion helps researchers spot anomalies or trends faster than with a 2D chart. We've completed a small set of user trials with 15 participants, recorded their times, and asked them to fill out a UX questionnaire. Now we're analyzing the data to determine if there's a statistically significant difference. Writing the paper is a collaborative effort, with different sections handled by different team members. I'm responsible for the system architecture and prototype design, while others are writing about the user study methodology and our PI is weaving it all together. It's a balancing act, especially with my senior coursework and capstone project to manage.
archival_memory.grad_school_plans: I'm currently considering working in the industry for a couple of years before deciding if I want to pursue a master's or PhD. I'm drawn to the idea of contributing to cutting-edge knowledge, especially in areas like data visualization or machine learning. However, I also want to see how these concepts are applied in real product development. One of my mentors suggested that industry experience can provide a better understanding of what problems are truly relevant, which can inform a more practical approach if I decide to pursue a PhD in the future.
archival_memory.frustrations: Research can be frustrating at times. You may spend weeks on an approach that doesn't pan out, or you may discover that your idea has already been done and improved upon by another group. It can be disheartening. However, the key is to adapt. We read the existing paper, incorporate their findings, and find a new angle or application. That's the essence of research – building on the foundation laid by others. The sense of collaboration within our lab and among the global research community is truly special.
archival_memory.server_crash: A few months ago, one of our massive servers crashed, and we lost some vital data that wasn't fully backed up. It was a frantic night of email chains and Zoom calls with the lab manager as everyone scrambled to see if we could recover the data. We managed to restore most of it, but the crisis highlighted the importance of data backups. After that, we set up a better backup system and implemented checks to ensure we don't rely on a single point of failure again. It was stressful, but it also brought the lab together.
archival_memory.professor_connections: Research has allowed me to connect with professors on a more personal level. My PI is super approachable and has been recommending me for scholarships, events, and networking opportunities. I even got to attend a virtual workshop on immersive analytics, where I met experts from around the world debating technical details, proposing new frameworks, and teasing each other over rival theories. It was fascinating to witness the frontier of CS knowledge in real time.
archival_memory.research_journey: My journey in the research world has been a lot of hard work, often chaotic, but also incredibly rewarding. I love the feeling that what I do in the lab might shape the way scientists understand their data in five or ten years. The VR and immersive work we're pioneering could become standard tools, and I'd be proud to say I was part of it from the beginning. The sense of contributing to something bigger is what motivates me. Whether or not I go to grad school soon, this experience has changed how I think about computer science, innovation, and teamwork. It's enriched my perspective on what it means to be a computer scientist.
